opus-5.5.text:
I think the core challenge is that the summary is lossy in ways that are really hard to predict ahead of time. When the model writes a summary of what it's tried, it has to decide what matters, and it often doesn't know yet which details will turn out to be important. So you'll see things like it records "I tried approach X and it didn't work," but it drops the specific error message or the subtle reason it failed. Then the next instance, starting fresh from that summary, either retries something almost identical, or it overcorrects and abandons a direction that was actually ninety percent of the way there.

There's also a kind of confidence problem. A summary reads as more authoritative than the raw trajectory. If an earlier attempt concluded "this library doesn't support that feature," and that conclusion was actually wrong, a misread of the docs, say, the summary bakes that mistake in as a fact. The fresh context has no way to second-guess it, because the evidence that might have revealed the error is gone.

And then there's just the question of what the model is good at. Models have mostly been trained to solve tasks within a single context, not to be good note-takers for a future version of themselves. Writing a handoff that's actually useful, capturing the state of the world, the dead ends, the open hypotheses, what you'd try next, is a skill, and humans aren't great at it either. Think about how hard it is to pick up a coworker's half-finished branch from their notes.

So in practice, what we've found helps is being more structured about it: having the agent keep a running progress file or notes as it goes rather than summarizing only at the end, preserving concrete artifacts like test results and actual error output rather than paraphrases, and leaning on the environment itself, the code, git history, the test suite, as the source of truth. The less you rely on the summary to carry the state, and the more it just points to where the state lives, the better it works.

r001.rationale: The response identifies lossy, unpredictable summaries as the core challenge: they can omit why approaches failed or preserve mistaken conclusions, leaving a fresh context without key evidence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core problem is that a summary is lossy in exactly the places you most need it not to be. When an agent has been working on something for a long time, say it's been trying to fix a bug for a few hundred thousand tokens, the really valuable information isn't "I tried approach A and it didn't work." It's the texture of why it didn't work. What the error message actually said, what the state of the code looked like at that moment, the half-formed hypothesis the agent had about the root cause. When you compress that into a few sentences, you tend to keep the conclusion and throw away the evidence.

And the failure mode we see is that the agent reads the summary, sees "approach A failed," and then either rediscovers the same dead end because it doesn't understand what made it a dead end, or it overcorrects and avoids an entire region of the solution space that was actually fine, just slightly misapplied the first time. So you get this weird thing where the agent is both repeating itself and being too timid at the same time.

The other challenge is that the model writing the summary doesn't know what the future is going to need. It's compressing with respect to its current understanding of the task. But the whole reason you're going past 200K is that the task turned out to be harder or different than expected, so the thing you thought was irrelevant twenty minutes ago is often the thing that matters now. That's a prediction problem, and models are decent at it but far from perfect.

So what we've found works better is not relying on a single summary as the only artifact. You want the agent to externalize state into the environment, so write things to files, leave notes, commit intermediate work, keep a running log of what's been tried with enough detail to be actionable. Then the summary becomes more of an index into that state rather than the state itself. The agent after context reset can go read the actual file, look at the actual test output, rather than trusting a paraphrase of it.

And honestly, part of the answer is just training the model to be good at this. Writing a summary that's useful to a future version of yourself with no memory is a skill, and it's one we can actually measure and improve. Early on, models would write summaries that sounded fine but were kind of useless, very high level, "made progress on the feature." Now they're much better at noting the specific things that would be costly to rediscover. But I'd say it's still one of the areas where there's a lot of headroom.

r001.rationale: The response identifies lossy summaries as the core problem and explains that they discard the evidence and details behind why attempted approaches failed, making it hard to continue work after a context reset.

astra-6.text:
I think the main challenge is that you don’t know ahead of time which details you’re going to need later. You can summarize an attempt as, “I tried this approach and it didn’t work,” but the useful information might be exactly why it didn’t work, or some observation you made along the way. If that gets lost, the agent can end up repeating the same mistake.

So the question is how to preserve enough of what the agent learned to make continued progress without just carrying the entire history forward. A summary can help, but it’s a lossy compression step, and doing that repeatedly can lose the details that matter.

r001.rationale: The response explains that summaries can lose useful details and cause repeated mistakes, but frames the challenge as preserving enough information. It does not clearly identify losslessly summarizing what the agent learned as the main challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main challenge is preserving the right information. You can summarize an attempted approach as “I tried this and it didn’t work,” but the useful part is often why it didn’t work—what assumption was wrong, what evidence you found, and whether some piece of that approach is still worth pursuing.

And you don’t necessarily know at summarization time which detail will matter later. If you throw away too much, the agent can end up repeating the same mistakes. If you preserve everything, you’re back to filling the context window. So the hard part is creating a compact memory that actually lets the agent build on its previous work.

r001.rationale: The response identifies preserving useful information about past attempts as the main challenge, but it does not clearly say the summary must preserve what the agent learned losslessly; it allows that some details may be discarded.
